question: What is the primary purpose of Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) in nursing practice?

options.A: To completely eliminate all microorganisms from the hospital environment
options.B: To prevent or minimize the risk of transmitting infectious agents to patients and staff
options.C: To ensure patients experience shorter hospital stays without medication
options.D: To reduce the cost of purchasing hospital equipment and supplies

explanation: IPC encompasses practices specifically designed to prevent or minimize the transmission of infectious agents to patients, healthcare workers, and visitors. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h1)

question: Which of the following describes how IPC practices stop the spread of infectious diseases?

options.A: By breaking one or more links in the chain of infection
options.B: By increasing the susceptibility of the host to pathogens
options.C: By encouraging microorganisms to find new reservoirs

explanation: Breaking any link in the chain of infection—such as the infectious agent, mode of transmission, or susceptible host—effectively stops the spread of disease. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h1)

question: Which of the following bloodborne pathogens is a major risk associated with unsafe injection practices?
explanation: Unsafe injection practices heavily contribute to the transmission of bloodborne pathogens, which include HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h2)

question: What is a core principle regarding the equipment used for administering an injection?

options.A: Needles and syringes may be reused if sterilized properly in boiling water
options.B: A sterile, single-use disposable syringe and needle must be used for every injection
options.C: Multidose vials can be accessed repeatedly using the same dispensing needle
options.D: Syringes can be shared among family members if washed thoroughly

explanation: Every injection requires a fresh, sterile, single-use disposable syringe and needle to prevent cross-contamination and pathogen transmission. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h2)

question: When should hand hygiene be performed in relation to wearing gloves?

options.A: Hand hygiene is not necessary if medical gloves are worn throughout the procedure
options.B: Hand hygiene must be performed immediately after removing gloves
options.C: Gloves should be washed with soap and water while still on the hands
options.D: Hand hygiene is only required before putting on sterile gloves

explanation: Gloves can have microscopic defects or become contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene must always be performed immediately after taking them off. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h3)

question: According to standard precautions, body substances from which of the following are assumed to be potentially infectious?

options.B: Blood, body fluids, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes
options.C: Excretions of healthy individuals without underlying medical conditions
options.D: Tears and saliva from pediatric patients only

explanation: Standard precautions apply to all body fluids, secretions, excretions (excluding sweat), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes, assuming potential infectious risk for everyone. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h3)

question: What action should a nurse take if a sterile needle accidentally touches an unsterilized surface?

options.A: Wipe it down thoroughly with an alcohol swab and use it
options.B: Discard the contaminated needle and syringe immediately
options.C: Rinse the needle under running tap water before use
options.D: Use it only for intramuscular injections where risk is lower

explanation: Once a sterile component touches a non-sterile surface, it is contaminated and must be discarded to prevent introducing pathogens into the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h4)

question: How should the skin at the injection site be prepared prior to administering an injection?

options.A: Wiped vigorously in a back-and-forth motion and dried with a tissue
options.B: Cleansed with an antiseptic wipe in a circular motion from the center outward and allowed to air dry
options.C: Washed thoroughly with ordinary soap and cold water
options.D: Left unprepared if the patient's skin appears clean

explanation: Skin preparation requires a circular motion from the center outward to push microbes away from the site, followed by complete air drying to ensure antiseptic efficacy. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the recommended practice regarding the recapping of used injection needles?

options.A: Always use a two-handed technique to ensure the cap fits securely
options.B: Never recap used needles, or use a safe one-handed scoop technique if unavoidable
options.C: Recap the needle firmly by pushing it against a hard table surface
options.D: Ask a colleague to hold the cap while you push the needle in

explanation: Two-handed recapping is a major cause of needle-stick injuries; needles should not be recapped, or a one-handed scoop method must be used if clinically necessary. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h5)

question: At what capacity should a sharps container be safely sealed and replaced?

options.A: When it is completely full to maximize container usage
options.B: When it reaches the three-quarters (75%) full mark
options.C: At the end of every working week regardless of fill level
options.D: When needles begin to poke out of the side walls

explanation: Sharps containers must be sealed and replaced when they reach three-quarters full to prevent accidental punctures and overfilling hazards. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h5)

question: What is the immediate first-aid action a nurse should take after experiencing a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Squeeze the wound vigorously to force out any contaminated blood
options.B: Wash the puncture site immediately with soap and water without scrubbing
options.C: Apply a strong disinfectant like concentrated bleach directly to the wound
options.D: Cover the wound tightly with an airtight bandage and continue working

explanation: The puncture site should be washed immediately with soap and water; scrubbing or squeezing should be avoided as it can increase tissue damage and pathogen absorption. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h6)

question: Within what timeframe should Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV ideally be initiated after a high-risk exposure?

options.D: Only after the source patient's laboratory results return in 6 months

explanation: HIV PEP is most effective when started as soon as possible after exposure, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h6)

question: How should a nurse address a patient who insists on receiving an injectable medication when an equivalent oral drug is appropriate?

options.A: Refuse to speak with the patient about their medication preferences
options.B: Educate the patient on the risks of unnecessary injections and the efficacy of oral options
options.C: Administer the injection anyway to maintain patient satisfaction
options.D: Tell the patient that injections are illegal in their specific health district

explanation: Nurses act as educators to correct misconceptions about injections, explaining the risks of unnecessary parenteral therapy and the benefits of oral alternatives. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h7)

question: What is an example of patient empowerment regarding injection safety?

options.A: Allowing patients to administer their own intravenous medications unsupervised
options.B: Educating patients to look for a fresh, sealed syringe opened in their presence
options.C: Instructing patients to bring their own needles from home for hospital procedures
options.D: Encouraging patients to recap their own needles after use

explanation: Empowering patients involves health literacy education, such as encouraging them to ensure syringes are newly opened from sterile packaging right in front of them. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h7)
